options.title: This piece of Russia doesn't touch Russia
options.first_line: This piece of Russia, on the Baltic Sea, doesn't touch the rest of Russia at all.
options.first_frame: The old map of the Baltic with one small piece of land filled with Russia's flag, its border tracing round in light, Poland and Lithuania plain around it and the rest of Russia far off to the east.

options.title: Kaliningrad is Russia, but it's cut off from Russia
options.first_line: Kaliningrad is part of Russia, yet it sits cut off from Russia, between Poland and Lithuania.
options.first_frame: A pin drops on the city of Kaliningrad on the Baltic coast, its region filled with Russia's flag, a KALININGRAD label writing on, with Poland's and Lithuania's flags filling the land on either side.

options.title: Russia's most western land is boxed in by Poland and Lithuania
options.first_line: Russia's most western land sits nowhere near Russia: Poland and Lithuania box it in.
options.first_frame: The whole of Russia stretched across the map in its flag, then the camera slides west past Lithuania to a small detached piece on the Baltic, lit in the same flag.

why: Russia is instantly recognisable from the flag on the map, and 'doesn't touch Russia' raises a how-is-that-possible question that neither the title nor the first line answers, while B and C already give away where it is and who boxes it in.
